The CPU by session dialog is cleaned up and pushed to `master` as f9ef162a. Workspace clippy is clean and all 522 TUI tests pass.

**1. Tabs look like buttons.** Tabs already used the same colours as buttons, but they were drawn as bare text one space apart, so they read as a line of text. Each machine label is now padded with two spaces on each side, the same as a button, so it shows as a separate coloured block. I made this change in the CPU dialog only. `TabStrip` and the other three tab strips (turn review, resume and one other) are unchanged.

**2. The dialog keeps its size.** The height used to come from whichever machine tab was selected. It now comes from the machine with the most rows, so switching tabs no longer resizes it. There is also a blank row between the tabs and the list.

**3. Hourly / Recent buttons on the right.** They are stacked beside the list using the existing `ButtonColumn` component. The chosen one shows a check mark, and Hourly is the default. The choice sets:
- the figure on each row, and on a parent row the "own" share;
- the machine totals and tab labels;
- the sort order.

**Decisions you may want to change:**
- **Rows show only the chosen figure,** for example `23% recent`, instead of both figures. The session menu still shows both.
- **The coverage note is hidden in Recent mode.** That note, for example `(14m)`, says how long the hourly average covers, so it means nothing for the recent figure.
- **A parent's "own" share follows the chosen metric.** It used to always show the recent figure, so I updated one existing test that expected that.

**Tests:** I added a test that switches tabs and checks the dialog stays the same size. It would have failed with the old code, because the two machines in it have different numbers of rows. The same test clicks Recent and then Hourly and checks the rows, totals, tab labels and the coverage note. I also regenerated the dialog golden file.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- `TabStrip` already used the button colours (`focus_control` and `actionable_chip`). Because the background colour covers every cell of a label, adding spaces to the label was enough to make each tab look like a button, with no change to the shared component.
- While the dialog is open, `render_changes.rs` decides when to redraw by comparing the report's lines. Those lines now depend on the chosen metric, so that check reads the metric from the dialog. Otherwise a change in the recent figure might not redraw the dialog in Recent mode.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

I rewrote the instructions to fit Claude Code's limit and pushed the change to `master` as d2365955c.

**The cause (confirmed):** Claude Code keeps only the first **2,048 characters** of a server's instructions. The text this session received stops after exactly 2,048 characters. On master the parent instructions were 2,175 characters, so the last sentence was lost. That sentence was "The user can see children in the Sub-agents workspace."

**What changed** (in `mj-worker/src/subagent_mcp.rs`): I kept every rule but rewrote it more tightly. The text is now 1,933 characters, about 115 under the limit. It is ordered from most to least important:
1. What to delegate and what to keep for yourself.
2. Implementing through children, when to keep a slice yourself, and what you own.
3. Collecting reports: use `wait`, nothing is pushed to you, and read the handback and `report_dir`.
4. Re-tasking a wrong handback once, then taking over.
5. How to brief a child.
6. Test suites, profiling, duplicate work, and when to reuse a child.
7. Parked and closed children, and the Sub-agents workspace.

If the text grows past the limit again, only the lifecycle details at the end would be lost.

I kept the phrase "instead of duplicating work", because an existing test (from fcbd178e) requires it.

**New check:** a test now fails if the Claude parent or child instructions are longer than 2,048 characters. It would have failed on the old text. The Codex version is exempt, because Codex has no such limit as far as I know, and its text adds a tool-discovery hint before the shared instructions. The child instructions are already under the limit; I did not measure them exactly, but the new test checks them.

**Checks:** all worker tests pass (646 in the main suite) and workspace clippy is clean.

**When you'll see it:** this session's instructions are still the old, cut-off text. They change once you run a worker built from this commit.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The cut-off came with no warning to the server. The model just saw "…" and didn't know what was missing. A length test is the only reliable guard, because MCP clients don't report truncation back.
- Putting the least important rules last means a future change that goes over the limit loses detail rather than core routing rules.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
root cause and fix #1257
Both children are running: one on the worker lock tests and one on the CLI logging test. Waiting for their reports.
Both children report confirmed causes, with stress reproductions before and after their fixes. Next I'm reviewing the diffs myself.

I fixed all three tests and pushed the change to master as c233a1fbc. That closed #1257, and I removed the `agent-in-progress` label.

## The two worker tests

**Cause (confirmed):** the issue's guess was right. A test drops the worker root's lock (a `flock`) and then takes it again straight away. A `flock` belongs to the open file, not to the process. If another test thread forks a process in that gap, the child holds a copy of the file and the lock until it calls `exec`. Marking the file close-on-exec does not help before then. So the second acquire fails with "a worker already owns".

A child forked in this way, and held before `exec` while the owner dropped, made the tests fail every time. The log is `.mj/agents/88ea…/fork-repro.log`.

**Production is not affected:** the worker takes the root owner once in `mj-worker/src/main.rs:342-353` and keeps it until `main` exits. It never releases it and takes it again. The login re-exec turns off close-on-exec only around `exec` itself, before the Tokio runtime starts.

**Fix (test code only):**
- A test helper retries the acquire for up to 2 seconds when the root is busy.
- Both tests now fork a child that holds the lock across the release. This makes the race happen on every run, so the regression check is reliable.

Before the fix, each test failed 1 of 1 times with the held child. After it, each passed 12 of 12 times.

## The CLI logging test

**Cause (confirmed):** `ReliableWriter::flush` waited only 1 second. Under load, a burst of 10,000 lines takes longer than that to write. No lines were lost and nothing was written out of order; the wait was just too short.

**This affected production too:** the same flush runs when the CLI's log guard is dropped at exit. When it timed out there, the process could exit with log lines still queued and never written.

**Fix:** the flush now waits up to 10 seconds. Before the fix, a run with one CPU and heavy load failed 8 of 8 times. After it, the same run passed 8 of 8 times, taking 4.5 to 6.5 seconds.

**Checks:** the children ran the full test suites and clippy for both crates, and all passed.

**Not checked:** I did not rerun the full parallel workspace command from the issue (`mbx test --workspace …`). If one of these tests fails again under a full run, check that the 10-second flush limit is not being reached in normal use.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Close-on-exec closes a file only at `exec`. Between `fork` and `exec`, every open file belongs to the child as well. For locks tied to the open file, like `flock`, the child holds the lock during that time. Production avoids the problem by never releasing the lock and taking it again.
- Holding a forked child at the exact moment the lock is released turns a rare race into one that happens every time. That makes the regression test reliable instead of hoping the scheduler hits the gap.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Jev should always recover from a confident quota stop, even when it also thinks the agent is waiting for the user.

Incident: worker 0bf0983d553751026807d97d54857ede, 2026-10-06 12:17:41 to 12:23:17 CDT. Seven assessments (ordinals 41873, 41880, 41888, 41896, 41903, 41911, 41919) in ~/.local/share/mjolnir/workers/0bf0983d553751026807d97d54857ede/jev-decisions/decisions.0.jsonl. Each one had failure=quota at 1.0 ("You've hit your session limit · resets 3pm"), input=required at 0.82 to 0.89, and action=await_input with no retry time. The session never resumed after the reset. The input=required verdict was probably caused by an opt-out line in the last reply ("Tell me if you want to hold the push instead."), but the cause does not matter here. We cannot make question detection reliable, and the resumed agent can stop and ask again if it really needs a decision.

Cause: Verdict::action in mj-core/src/assessment.rs checks requires_input() before the failure branch, so AwaitInput wins over RecoverQuota. The test explicit_user_handoff_blocks_provider_automation locks in that order for quota.

Change:
1. In Verdict::action, return RecoverQuota whenever failure.choice is Quota with confidence >= AUTOMATION_CONFIDENCE, before the requires_input() check, whatever the input and work answers are. Leave TransientProvider and Other as they are. Low-confidence quota keeps its current behavior.
2. Find the prompt the worker sends when a quota recovery comes due (start at mj-worker/src/relay/verdict.rs, the Action::RecoverQuota arm, and mj-worker/src/relay/commands.rs). Make sure it tells the agent that if it was waiting on a user decision before the limit, it should ask again and stop instead of proceeding. If continuation::PROMPT is the prompt used and already says this, leave it alone.
3. Check every other place that combines requires_input() with failure or quota handling, so none of them still blocks quota recovery:
   - mj-core/src/activity/verdict.rs (around line 218)
   - mj-core/src/relay/snapshot/apply.rs (around lines 240 and 1434)
   - mj-controller/src/daemon/continuation.rs (around lines 321 and 713)
   - scripts/jev-scenarios-eval.py (requires_input and the action policy around lines 55 to 65). This is a Python copy of the Rust policy and must match it.
   - mj-core/tests/jev_scenarios.rs and its fixtures. Update any expected action for quota + required.
4. Tests:
   - Change explicit_user_handoff_blocks_provider_automation so that Quota + Required gives RecoverQuota. Transient + Required must still give AwaitInput.
   - Add a regression test shaped like the incident: quota at 1.0, input required at 0.89 (none 0.10, redundant_request 0.01), work split about evenly between authorized_unfinished, finished and waiting, and authorization_complete true. It must give RecoverQuota.
   - Run the affected mj-core, mj-worker and mj-controller tests, plus scripts/jev-scenarios-eval.test.py.

Jev now resumes after a confident quota stop even when it also thinks the agent is waiting for the user. All requested tests pass, and the change is committed as `91ef9d506` on `master` (not pushed).

**The recovery prompt is unchanged.** When a quota recovery comes due, the daemon sends `RelayCommand::ResumeAfterQuota` (`mj-controller/src/daemon/continuation/quota.rs:339`). `RelayCommand::prompt_blocks` turns that into `continuation::prompt_blocks()` (`mj-core/src/relay/snapshot.rs:164`), so the agent receives `continuation::PROMPT` (`mj-core/src/continuation.rs:12`):

> "Continue the unfinished work already requested by the user, following their latest instructions. This message supplies no new approval or missing information. If a genuine decision, required approval, or external action remains necessary, explain it and stop."

The last sentence already tells the agent to ask again and stop if a decision is still open, so I left the prompt alone as you asked. One exception: if the session has a goal that can resume after quota, the daemon sends `GoalControl::Resume` instead, and that path sends no prompt. That path is outside this change.

**Files changed:**
- `mj-core/src/assessment.rs`:
  - `Verdict::action` now returns `RecoverQuota` first when the failure is quota with confidence at or above `AUTOMATION_CONFIDENCE`.
  - `TransientProvider`, `Other` and low-confidence quota keep their old behavior.
  - I renamed the test to `explicit_user_handoff_blocks_provider_retry_but_not_quota_recovery`. Quota + Required now gives `RecoverQuota`, Transient + Required still gives `AwaitInput`, and quota at 0.89 + Required gives `AwaitInput`.
  - I added a `// Hard-won: 8cecc1c` marker; that is the commit that introduced the old order.
- `mj-core/tests/jev-gates.json`: added the incident case (quota 1.0; input required 0.89 / none 0.10 / redundant_request 0.01; work split 0.35 / 0.32 / 0.33; authorization complete; expected `recover_quota`). Both the Rust test and the Python test read this file, so this one case checks both copies of the policy.
- `scripts/jev-scenarios-eval.py`: `action()` now matches the Rust order.
- `scripts/jev-scenarios-eval.test.py`: added quota + required checks at 0.99 (gives `recover_quota`) and at 0.89 (gives `await_input`). I renamed the test, since "required input beats everything" is no longer true.

**The other places you listed needed no change:**
- `mj-controller/src/daemon/continuation.rs` (lines 321 and 713): both read the stored `a.action`, so they follow the new order automatically. The older path uses `is_quota_limit()`, which never checked input.
- `mj-core/src/relay/snapshot/apply.rs` (lines 240 and 1434): they only check whether the action is `RecoverQuota`. They do not check input.
- `mj-core/tests/jev_scenarios.rs` fixtures: no recorded scenario combines quota with required input. The quota fixtures (S23, S24, S27) still pass.
- `mj-core/src/activity/verdict.rs:218`: for a finished turn it uses `action()`, so quota now leads to `KeepCurrent`. While a turn is still running, `requires_input()` alone still gives `AwaitingInput`. I left that alone because it does not block recovery: the worker schedules quota recovery from the assessment it makes after the turn ends (`apply_turn_assessment`), and that now gives `RecoverQuota`. Change it too if you also want a quota stop during a running turn to suppress the "waiting for input" status.

**Tests (run by a child agent):**
- `mj-core`: full crate, 465 unit tests and 2 scenario tests passed.
- `mj-worker`: tests matching `relay` (333) and `verdict` (25) passed.
- `mj-controller`: tests matching `continuation` (21) passed.
- `scripts/jev-scenarios-eval.test.py`: 19 tests passed.
- `cargo clippy -p brokk-mj-core --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` passed.

The Cargo package names are `brokk-mj-*`, so `cargo test -p mj-core` does not find a package. I did not run workspace-wide clippy.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The decision is made in one place. `Verdict::action` produces the action; the worker stores it, and the controller and the snapshot code only read the stored value. That is why fixing one function fixed every downstream site, and why `continuation.rs` needed no edit.
- `jev-gates.json` is the shared contract between the Rust policy and its Python copy. Putting the incident there, rather than in two separate unit tests, means the two copies cannot quietly disagree on this case.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
